assessed.title: Randomised controlled trial to investigate an online compassionate imagery intervention for improving veterinarian mental wellbeing.
assessed.abstract: Background Veterinarians are at increased risk of psychological distress due to the regular experience of moral dilemmas, leading to compassion fatigue and burnout. This study explored the efficacy of a 2-week, modified online compassionate imagery intervention for improving veterinarian mental wellbeing. Methods A randomised controlled trial design was used with two parallel arms (intervention vs. wait-list control group). One hundred and sixty-two students and qualified veterinarians were randomly allocated to each arm. The intervention group watched a 10-15-minute video every day for 14 days to increase their self-compassion. Participants completed questionnaires to measure outcomes across four time points (baseline, immediately post-intervention, and 1- and 2-month follow-ups). Results One hundred and one participants were included in the analysis of variance. The intervention significantly improved resilience (F[2, 198] = 4.39, p = 0.014, ηp2  = 0.043), self-reassurance (F[2, 198] = 4.61, p = 0.01, ηp2  = 0.045), self-compassion (F[2, 198] = 8.80, p ≤ 0.001, ηp2  = 0.08), work-related rumination (distraction detachment: F[2, 198] = 4.92, p = 0.008, ηp2  = 0.047, problem-solving pondering: F[1.86, 184.82] = 5.88, p = 0.004, ηp2  = 0.056) and self-criticism (F[1.80, 136.94] = 3.60, p = 0.03, ηp2  = 0.045). These findings were sustained at follow-up and were associated with small-to-medium and medium-to-large effect sizes. Limitations Randomisation was not entirely successful. Due to missing data, an intention-to-treat analysis was not feasible, raising the possibility of an inflated treatment effect. Blinding was not possible due to resource constraints. Conclusions An online compassionate imagery intervention was efficacious at improving multiple outcomes associated with veterinarian mental wellbeing. These findings provide a rationale for developing and delivering compassion-based interventions to veterinarians.
assessed.exclusion_note: Burnout mentioned only as background; the reported outcomes are resilience, self-compassion, rumination and self-criticism

assessed.title: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Social Support Intervention Effects on Stress and Burnout in School-Based Speech-Language Pathologists.
assessed.abstract: Purpose Social support is an interpersonal resource with established effects on reducing occupational stress and burnout. Unlike typically recommended self-care and self-awareness techniques, social support can be directly implemented in the workplace and serves as an effective buffer against job-related stressors. This study aimed to determine how social support influences reported occupational stress and burnout symptoms among speech-language pathologists (SLPs). Method We developed and implemented a social support group program called Peer Support for School-based Speech-Language Therapists, using a randomized control trial design. Forty-six school-based SLPs were randomly assigned to either an immediate or delayed treatment group and participated in weekly social support group sessions online for 6 weeks. Pretest, posttest, and delayed posttest scores on the SLP Stress Inventory and the Maslach Burnout Inventory: Educators Survey were compared. Results Changes across postintervention and delayed postintervention for the treatment group were observed. A significant difference was found between each time point for total stress scores and for emotional exhaustion scores. The mean total stress score was significantly reduced between baseline intervention and postintervention and then increased slightly at delayed postintervention. The data did not reveal significant posttest differences between the treatment and delayed treatment groups. Conclusions The positive feedback provided by the participants suggests that access to additional peer support can be equally important to the management of stress and burnout symptoms. Implications, limitations, and future directions of this work are discussed. Supplemental material https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.33989560.

assessed.title: Factors influencing implementation of a digital compassion training program: Findings from a Randomized Waitlist-Controlled Trial (Preprint)
assessed.abstract: BACKGROUND Digital mental health interventions are increasingly used to address stress, burnout, and well-being among working adults because they offer scalable and accessible approaches to psychological support. Although digitally delivered compassion training programs show promise, implementation outcomes such as feasibility, acceptability, and participant-perceived fit remain underexamined. In particular, little is known about the extent to which digital compassion interventions help participants achieve the outcomes they most hope to gain through participation. OBJECTIVE This study evaluated the feasibility, acceptability, and expectation-outcome alignment of Compassion U, a blended care adaptation of Cognitively Based Compassion Training (CBCT®) program tailored for healthcare, education, and business professionals. Exploratory analyses examined potential signals of change in compassion-related and well-being outcomes. METHODS A pilot randomized waitlist-controlled trial was conducted with 137 participants from healthcare (n=46), business (n=54), and education (n=37) professions. Participants were randomized to either Compassion U or a waitlist control condition. The intervention combined asynchronous mobile-accessible CBCT modules with weekly live instructor-facilitated sessions over 10 weeks. Primary implementation outcomes included feasibility, acceptability assessed using the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability (TFA), and expectation-outcome alignment. Expectation fulfillment was quantified using a novel Expectation Fulfillment Index (EFI), representing the proportion of participants’ desired baseline outcomes subsequently perceived as having benefited from the intervention. Exploratory outcome analyses examined compassion, well-being, loneliness, stress, emotion regulation, and workplace-related outcomes. RESULTS Feasibility was supported by successful recruitment across all three professional sectors and retention rates comparable to those reported in digital mental health intervention studies. Participants demonstrated high baseline readiness to engage with the intervention, with no significant readiness differences observed across sectors. Acceptability was high at postintervention (overall acceptability score: mean 4.33/5) and remained favorable at follow-up. Participants reported broadly positive perceived benefits across domains. The mean EFI was 0.58 (SD 0.41); however, expectation fulfillment was highly heterogeneous, with 30.6% of participants reporting high benefits to desired outcomes and 27.8% reporting no benefits. Personal growth, self-compassion, and mental health were among the most frequently endorsed desired outcomes, whereas professional development demonstrated the largest expectation-benefit gap. Expectation fulfillment was most strongly associated with participant motivation and commitment to continued practice, suggesting that participant-defined goal attainment may represent an important but often overlooked dimension of success in digital mental health interventions. Consistent with the pilot nature of the study, exploratory effectiveness analyses identified 2 notable outcome signals favoring the intervention: increased beliefs in the malleability of compassion (Hedges g=0.70, 95% CI 0.26-1.13) and reduced loneliness (Hedges g=−0.55, 95% CI −0.97 to −0.11). Most other outcomes demonstrated small or negligible effects, and observed effects generally attenuated by follow-up. CONCLUSIONS Compassion U demonstrated strong feasibility and acceptability across healthcare, education, and business professionals and was perceived as beneficial in several domains prioritized by participants. Findings suggest that expectation-outcome alignment and expectation fulfillment provide useful participant-centered indicators of intervention fit and participant-defined goal attainment that complement traditional implementation and effectiveness outcomes. The association between expectation fulfillment and participant motivation further suggests that intervention success may be shaped not only by program use, but also by the extent to which participants remain invested in personally meaningful goals. Future fully powered trials should further evaluate expectation fulfillment as a participant-centered lens for understanding how individuals experience and evaluate digital mental health interventions.
assessed.exclusion_note: Unpublished preprint of a pilot trial with implementation outcomes

assessed.title: Effect of Virtual Reality Relaxation on Alarm Fatigue and Professional Quality of Life Among Nurses in Intensive Care Units
assessed.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction Intensive care unit nurses are faced with a large number of equipment alarms daily, which can increase the likelihood of errors and threaten their professional quality of life. Today, the use of virtual reality to create relaxing experiences in stressful environments has received attention. This study aimed to determine the effect of virtual reality relaxation on alarm fatigue and the professional quality of life among ICU nurses. Methods This is an intervention study with a pretest‐posttest design with a control group. ICU nurses who met the inclusion criteria were selected conveniently and were randomly assigned to two intervention and control groups (30 people in each group). The intervention was implemented as three 20‐min virtual reality relaxation sessions over a week. The data collection tools included the Alarm Fatigue Scale (AFS) and the Professional Quality of Life (ProQOL) questionnaire. The questionnaires were completed before and immediately after the intervention. Results The results showed that the mean AFS score improved significantly after the intervention ( p < 0.001), and there was a significant difference between the intervention and control groups ( p = 0.014). The mean dimensions of ProQOL also improved significantly in all three dimensions of compassion satisfaction, burnout, and secondary trauma stress after the intervention ( p < 0.001). There was a significant difference between two groups in all dimensions after the intervention ( p < 0.001). Conclusion The significant improvement in AFS and ProQOL scores indicates that the use of new technologies, such as virtual reality can be considered as a complementary tool in promoting the mental and professional health of nurses in stressful environments.

assessed.title: A Personalized Recovery Intervention to Support Sleep Health in Emergency Healthcare Professionals.
assessed.abstract: Optimizing sleep health in healthcare professionals is a challenge, as misalignment between endogenous circadian rhythms and exogenous work schedules undermines recovery, well-being, and performance. This study evaluated a tailored recovery intervention based on cognitive-behavioural approaches for insomnia designed to support recovery to rotating night shifts. In a randomized controlled trial (REST), 72 emergency healthcare professionals were randomized to intervention or control. The intervention combined personalized sleep-wake feedback with stress management techniques. Sleep-wake rhythms were monitored via actigraphy for 3 weeks before and 1 week after the intervention. Outcomes included objective sleep duration, self-reported sleepiness, insomnia severity, and subjective sleep quality, measured using the Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Insomnia Severity Index, and Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire. Fifty-nine participants (28 intervention, 31 control) were included in the primary analyses. Even on free nights, average nocturnal sleep duration was 6 h and 21 min, below recommended levels for adults. Compared with controls, intervention participants increased nocturnal time in bed by 37 min, 95% CI [13, 62], p = 0.003, and total sleep time by 23 min, 95% CI [4, 42], p = 0.019. Perceived sleep quality also improved for the intervention group t(55) = -7.91, p < 0.001, d = 2.06, 95% CI [1.42, 2.70], and insomnia symptoms decreased (β = -2.23, 95% CI [-4.26, -0.21], p = 0.031). These findings suggest that structured occupational recovery programs can enhance sleep health and facilitate recovery across rotating night work schedules. Integrating such interventions into training may reduce burnout, improve safety, and support workforce sustainability.
assessed.exclusion_note: Sleep outcomes only; burnout appears only as a hoped-for consequence in the conclusion

assessed.title: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study Comparing ChatGPT to Live Coaching Deliberate Practice to Teach Difficult Conversations.
assessed.abstract: Poor performance during difficult conversations is associated with decreased patient satisfaction and increased clinician burnout. Communication skills can be taught using simulated patients (SPs), but this approach is resource intensive. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a potential adjunct for communication training. However, its role within anesthesiology education and structured communication curricula remains unclear. We conducted a randomized controlled pilot study involving anesthesiology trainees, including anesthesiology residents and student registered nurse anesthetists, at a tertiary pediatric hospital. All participants completed a didactic session on the SPIKES framework, followed by deliberate practice using either OpenAI's ChatGPT or an SP with live instructor feedback. Participants completed pretraining and posttraining assessments using a validated 16-item communication skills checklist with an SP. Self-reported knowledge, confidence, and ability to apply communication skills were assessed using Likert-scale surveys. Twenty-five trainees were enrolled (ChatGPT n = 13; SP n = 12). Both groups demonstrated significant improvements in checklist scores following training. Self-reported knowledge, confidence, and application of communication skills improved in both groups. A curriculum combining didactic instruction with deliberate practice using either ChatGPT or SPs was associated with improved simulated communication performance among anesthesiology trainees. This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of incorporating AI-based tools into communication training.
assessed.exclusion_note: Burnout mentioned only as background; outcomes are communication skills
